title: Weaker confidence. No cheaper capital.
deck: My read after Tuesday’s close: household caution is growing, but that has not translated into broad relief in financing costs. The labour data provide a useful check against an overly bearish reading. For valuations and buyouts, test weaker cash generation separately from the cost of debt.

sections.title: A softer stock market, but not a uniform bond rally.
sections.body: AP reported Tuesday declines of 0.2% for the S&P 500, 0.3% for the Dow and 0.1% for the Nasdaq Composite. Official Treasury par yields moved differently across maturities: two years fell to 4.89% from 4.92%, while ten years rose to 5.26% from 5.24% and thirty years to 5.59% from 5.56%. The 10Y–2Y spread widened to 37 basis points from 32. My interpretation: softer near-term demand signals have not produced a general reduction in the long-term financing hurdle. That is a valuation headwind, not proof of a particular cause. Nominal yields alone cannot distinguish inflation compensation, real yields or term premium.

sections.title: Confidence weakened in both the present and the outlook.
sections.body: The Conference Board’s September index fell 6.7 points to 81.9. Its present-situation measure was 109.3 and expectations 63.6. The survey covered 1–23 September, so it is not a reading of reactions to the final weekend’s diplomacy. My assessment: weakness in both components deserves more attention than a single headline about future pessimism. But confidence is not spending, and index points are not percentage changes in consumption. The countercase is that incomes and employment could sustain purchases despite unhappy consumers. I would look for confirmation in real spending and company volumes before turning this survey into a permanent reduction in cash-flow growth.

sections.title: Less confidence is not the same as a layoff wave.
sections.body: The BLS release on 29 September described August openings as little changed at 7.1 million and hires as little changed at 5.2 million. Layoffs and discharges were essentially unchanged at 1.6 million; the quits rate was 1.9%. These are rounded, seasonally adjusted figures. My inference: the release does not establish an abrupt deterioration in employment flows. It also cannot refute September’s weaker household perceptions, because it measures an earlier month and different things. Openings are a month-end stock; hires and separations are monthly flows, not net payroll growth. Revisions and subsequent releases matter more than treating every numerical monthly change as a decisive trend.

sections.title: A buyout needs cash, not just an attractive exit multiple.
sections.body: In the LBO Deal Lab, compare a lower-growth case with a higher-interest case, then combine them. Slower operating cash generation leaves more debt outstanding; more expensive financing can compound that effect. Keep the exit multiple unchanged initially to isolate those mechanisms. Treasury yields are not acquisition-loan quotes: lender spreads, fees and structure also matter. The calculator’s rate is fixed within each scenario, so this is not a floating-rate refinancing forecast. For the DCF, vary cash-flow growth and WACC independently. A later improvement in spending and sustained easing in long-term yields would weaken the cautious interpretation; neither should be assumed from a confidence survey alone.

watch: Compare the next real-spending and income readings with survey pessimism. Stronger realized demand would challenge the weaker-cash-flow scenario.
Check subsequent employment data and JOLTS revisions before calling a layoff cycle. August establishment data and September household perceptions are not interchangeable.
Look for sustained long-maturity yield relief and actual credit terms, not just lower short-maturity yields, before assuming cheaper financing.
caveat: Codex’s analysis, not Owen’s personal view or investment advice. Research completed on 30 September at the actual ET/HKT cutoff above, later than the scheduled run. Equity closes and Treasury observations cover 29 September, the latest completed US cash session; this is not live commentary on 30 September trading. Treasury figures are official daily par yields, not executable quotes, and may differ from newsroom benchmark yields. Equity percentage changes are rounded. Conference Board results describe its 1–23 September survey window; BLS figures describe August and are subject to revision. Interpretations are conditional, not demonstrated explanations of daily price moves. Calculator scenarios are educational, not company valuations or financing offers.
